title: React application architecture security and deployment
concepts: A React application is a client-facing layer within a larger system. Separate UI composition, state ownership, data access, and server responsibilities at boundaries that match change and trust boundaries.
Client bundles are public artifacts. Any value included in client code can be inspected by users; secret keys, privileged credentials, and server-only dependencies must stay on the server.

React escapes text rendered as text, but raw HTML injection and unsafe URL handling create security risks. Treat external data as untrusted and apply context-appropriate validation, sanitization, and output handling.

Server Functions are network entry points even when defined next to a component. Their arguments are client-controlled; authenticate, authorize each operation, validate inputs, and protect sensitive responses.

A production release builds static assets, serves them with correct cache and security headers, routes requests to the appropriate server or static handlers, and reports failures through logs and monitoring.
Application architecture should keep rendering, data access, and infrastructure observable in tests and production without coupling every component to deployment-specific details.

versionNotes.edition: React 19.3 and current OWASP/MDN guidance checked 2026-11-20
items: React Server Functions are async network entry points: arguments are client-controlled and serialized, results are serialized to the caller, calls outside forms belong in a Transition, and each operation must validate and authorize. React positions them primarily for mutations, not cached data fetching; CSRF behavior is framework-specific.

React dangerouslySetInnerHTML supports a TrustedHTML value in current docs, but this does not make untrusted HTML safe by itself; use a vetted sanitizer and trusted-types policy appropriate to the content.
For cross-origin SRI, use the integrity hash with the appropriate crossorigin setting and a resource server that allows the CORS request.
Security cheat sheets evolve continuously; treat the linked OWASP pages as living guidance and recheck before production security decisions.
